title: Purpose and organization of acute inflammation
sections: Acute inflammation is an early protective response to tissue injury. Its vascular and cellular components bring plasma proteins and leukocytes to the affected site, helping contain the injury and begin the process of tissue repair.

Infection is one possible trigger, but inflammation can also follow sterile injury. Physical trauma, tissue necrosis and irritating substances can activate inflammatory pathways even when microorganisms are absent from the injured tissue.

Resident cells detect danger locally before large numbers of circulating cells arrive. Tissue macrophages and other sentinel cells release signals that change nearby vessels and help organize the recruitment of additional defensive cells.

The response has a coordinated sequence rather than a single isolated event. Recognition of injury leads to mediator release, vascular changes, leukocyte recruitment, removal of harmful material and, when possible, resolution and repair.

Redness and warmth reflect increased local blood flow. Swelling reflects fluid accumulation in tissue. Pain and impaired function can accompany the process, but these features do not identify the exact cause of an inflammatory response by themselves.

Neutrophils are prominent early cells in many acute inflammatory responses. They can move from blood into tissue and participate in antimicrobial defense, while their enzymes and reactive products can also injure surrounding host tissue.

Inflammation must be localized and regulated to remain useful. A response that is too weak may fail to contain injury, while an excessive or persistent response can contribute to tissue damage instead of restoring normal function.

Anatomical location changes how inflammation appears and affects function. The same broad mechanisms operate in different tissues, but fluid accumulation, cell recruitment and subsequent repair must be interpreted within the structure of the affected organ.

title: Vascular events and fluid movement
sections: Arteriolar dilation increases blood delivery to an injured area. More blood enters the local microcirculation, contributing to the redness and warmth of acute inflammation and providing a vascular route for additional defensive components to reach the site.

Increased vascular permeability allows fluid and plasma proteins to move into the interstitial space. This is distinct from simply increasing blood flow, because the vessel wall must also permit material to cross from blood into tissue.

Protein-rich inflammatory fluid is called an exudate. A transudate is comparatively low in protein and usually reflects altered pressure relationships rather than the same permeability changes that produce a typical inflammatory exudate.

Fluid movement depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces as well as the vessel wall. Inflammation changes several of these relationships, so edema cannot be explained solely by saying that more blood has entered the region.

Loss of fluid from the vascular space can concentrate cells within smaller vessels. Slower blood movement and increased local viscosity contribute to stasis, which changes how circulating leukocytes interact with the endothelial surface.

Margination describes movement of leukocytes toward the edge of the flowing blood column. Their proximity to the vessel wall helps prepare the subsequent rolling and adhesion steps that precede movement into inflamed tissue.

Postcapillary venules are important sites for leukocyte recruitment and increased permeability in many acute responses. Vessel type and location therefore matter when following a white cell from the circulation to the site of tissue injury.

A schematic vessel model can separate lumen, endothelium and surrounding tissue. Fluid leakage and cell migration should be explained as different processes, even though both contribute to bringing defensive material out of blood and into an injured area.

title: Leukocyte recruitment and diapedesis
sections: Leukocyte recruitment proceeds through a sequence of interactions. Margination brings cells near the vessel wall; rolling permits transient contact; firm adhesion stabilizes attachment; transmigration allows passage through the wall; and chemotaxis guides movement within tissue.

Rolling depends on transient adhesive interactions that repeatedly form and break. These contacts slow a leukocyte along the endothelial surface without immediately fixing it in one position, creating an opportunity for subsequent activating signals.

Selectins contribute to the rolling phase of recruitment. These interactions differ from the stronger adhesive contacts of firm adhesion, so a rolling leukocyte should not be described as already permanently attached to the vessel wall.

Chemokines can activate leukocytes and increase the affinity of their integrins. The cell then forms stronger contacts with endothelial adhesion molecules, helping convert a moving rolling interaction into stable attachment before crossing the endothelial barrier.

Diapedesis refers to leukocyte passage across the vessel wall. It follows adhesive preparation and should be distinguished from movement through the interstitial tissue, which takes place after the cell has left the vascular compartment.

A cell crossing the endothelium changes its relationship to the vessel lumen and the surrounding tissue. A teaching model should make these compartments explicit so that movement through an endothelial gap is not confused with movement along the vessel surface.

Chemotaxis is directed movement along chemical gradients. Signals from microbes and inflamed tissue help guide recruited cells toward the relevant site, rather than leaving them to disperse randomly after crossing the vessel wall.

The sequence can fail at different steps. A problem with rolling, firm adhesion, transmigration or directed movement can reduce effective recruitment, even when the circulating blood contains cells that would otherwise be capable of participating in defense.

title: Inflammatory signals and mediators
sections: Inflammatory mediators coordinate vascular and cellular events. Some are stored and released rapidly, while others must be synthesized after stimulation. Their timing helps explain why different components of the response do not occur simultaneously.

Histamine is a rapidly acting mediator associated with vascular changes. Its contribution should be connected to vessel dilation and permeability rather than treating it as a complete explanation for every component of an inflammatory response.

Prostaglandins are lipid mediators derived from arachidonic acid through cyclooxygenase pathways. Different prostaglandins have different actions, so the family should not be described as a single molecule producing one uniform effect in all tissues.

Leukotrienes are another family of arachidonic-acid-derived mediators. Their effects include roles in leukocyte recruitment and changes in vascular or airway behavior, depending on the particular mediator and the tissue in which it acts.

Cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-1 help activate endothelial and other cells during inflammation. Local signaling can influence leukocyte recruitment, while broader mediator release can contribute to systemic features of a substantial response.

Chemokines form a group of signaling molecules that influence cell movement. Their spatial distribution helps organize recruitment and positioning, making the idea of a chemical gradient important when explaining why leukocytes move toward a particular area.

Complement links recognition of harmful material to several defensive effects. Its products can contribute to recruitment, coating of targets and membrane injury, but these functions are carried out by different components rather than one interchangeable complement molecule.

Mediator activity is regulated by production, receptor interactions, local distribution and inactivation. Limiting these signals is part of controlling inflammation, because persistent mediator activity can sustain vascular changes and recruitment after the original protective need has declined.

title: Phagocytosis and tissue defense
sections: Recruited leukocytes must recognize relevant targets before engulfing them. Recognition and attachment precede enclosure of material, so phagocytosis should be taught as an organized cellular process rather than simply a cell moving next to a microbe.

Opsonization improves recognition of a target by coating its surface with molecules that phagocytes can bind. Immunoglobulins and complement components can contribute to this process, linking target recognition to the receptors on defensive cells.

During engulfment, the phagocyte surrounds the attached target and brings it into an intracellular compartment. This creates a phagosome, separating the ingested material from the surrounding tissue while preparing it for subsequent intracellular processing.

Fusion with lysosomal compartments exposes ingested material to degradative mechanisms. The resulting phagolysosomal environment supports destruction and digestion, but the mechanisms involved should be distinguished from the earlier steps of adhesion and engulfment.

Reactive oxygen products contribute to microbial killing. Their generation is associated with the respiratory burst, a change in cellular metabolic activity that helps provide defensive chemistry within activated phagocytes after appropriate stimulation.

Oxygen-independent mechanisms also contribute to defense. Lysosomal enzymes and other antimicrobial components help process harmful material, showing that the protective activity of a phagocyte cannot be reduced to a single reactive molecule or pathway.

Defensive products can damage host structures if released or directed inappropriately. The same response that helps contain a microbial threat may contribute to tissue injury, which explains the importance of localization and regulation of leukocyte activity.

After the immediate response, dead cells and residual material must be cleared. This cleanup supports resolution and prepares the site for repair, connecting the cellular defense phase to the later restoration or remodeling of tissue.

title: Resolution, repair and patterns of inflammation
sections: Resolution becomes possible when the injurious stimulus is removed and the inflammatory response is controlled. Restoration requires more than stopping recruitment: excess fluid, dead cells and remaining debris also need to be cleared from the affected area.

Apoptosis helps remove spent neutrophils without requiring uncontrolled rupture of the cells. Their subsequent clearance by phagocytes supports termination of the response and reduces the unnecessary release of potentially damaging intracellular material into surrounding tissue.

Lymphatic drainage contributes to removal of excess interstitial fluid and material. This makes lymphatic function part of the overall management of tissue fluid, alongside the vascular changes that initially allowed fluid and proteins to leave the bloodstream.

Repair depends on the extent of injury and the capacity of the affected tissue to regenerate. Some tissue architecture can be restored, while more extensive destruction or limited regenerative capacity may lead to a greater contribution from scar formation.

Persistent injury can sustain inflammation and lead to a chronic response. The cellular composition and tissue consequences can change over time, so acute and chronic inflammation should not be treated merely as two labels for identical processes.

Purulent inflammation involves accumulation of pus containing inflammatory cells and tissue debris. An abscess is a localized collection within tissue, and its structure should be related to the underlying destructive and defensive events rather than just its surface appearance.

Fibrinous inflammation reflects deposition of fibrin in an inflammatory setting. It should be distinguished from a fluid-dominated serous pattern and from a purulent pattern, because these descriptions emphasize different material accumulated at the affected site.

The outcome of inflammation reflects the interaction between the initial injury, the effectiveness of defense and the capacity for recovery. Following this sequence connects recognition, vascular events, cell recruitment, target removal and repair into one coherent mechanism.
